# ADR-010: Django Database Role Is Generated by the Policy Compiler

## Status

Proposed

## Date

2026-08-07

## Context

The project's governance claim is that access control is enforced at the database layer, retrieval layer, and capability layer from a single policy manifest. An internal tool that connects as a superuser or bypasses row-level security would undercut that claim.

The Django-based ops console needs read access to review queues and must trigger state changes, but it must not become a parallel authority.

## Decision

`ops-console` uses a dedicated least-privilege database role. The role's GRANTs and RLS policies are generated by the M4.3 policy compiler from `policy-manifest.yaml`.

The role must not be a superuser, table owner, or bypass-RLS role. Django may read business tables through this role. State changes must call Java APIs, which perform authorization, audit, and writes through the established service path.

## Rejected Alternatives

| Alternative | Rejection reason |
|---|---|
| Connect Django as a database superuser | This bypasses RLS and contradicts the database-enforced governance model. |
| Define Django permissions separately | This creates a second policy source and violates the single-source-of-truth rule. |
| Allow Django to write business tables directly | This creates a second writer and splits audit-chain responsibility across two implementations. |
| Reuse an existing application database role | A dedicated role makes the console's permissions explicit and testable. |

## Consequences

The internal console becomes another demonstration of the policy compiler rather than an exception to it. The cost is extra policy generation, CI checks, and Java API endpoints for state transitions. This cost is justified because it preserves the governance architecture.
